topStories.headline: Cesar Chavez Street Set to Become 'Las Campesinas' Under New Ordinance
topStories.dek: District 9 Supervisor Jackie Fielder introduced legislation this week to rename the Mission's main artery, honoring the women of the farmworker movement.
topStories.body:
One of the Mission District's most-traveled streets may soon carry a new name. On Tuesday, District 9 Supervisor Jackie Fielder introduced an ordinance at the Board of Supervisors to rename Cesar Chavez Street as 'Las Campesinas' — Spanish for 'female farmworkers.' Supervisors Rafael Mandelman, Shamann Walton, and Myrna Melgar joined as co-sponsors. The legislation still needs to clear committee hearings and a full board vote before going to the mayor.

The push to rename the 3.5-mile corridor, which runs through the heart of the Mission, follows a New York Times investigation earlier this year that revealed Cesar Chavez had sexually abused women and girls over several decades. The street was previously called Army Street and was renamed in 1995 in honor of the United Farm Workers leader.

The new name was selected by a 27-member working group convened by Mayor Daniel Lurie and co-chaired by Assessor-Recorder Joaquin Torres and former Supervisor Susan Leal, who helped lead the original 1990s renaming effort. Two finalists — 'Las Campesinas' and 'Sí Se Puede' — were presented to the community at a meeting at Leonard R. Flynn Elementary School last month. More than 668 people submitted feedback online, and 'Las Campesinas' led by a significant margin.

The working group said the name is intended to honor the women — often unnamed and unseen — who worked the fields, organized their communities, and endured hardship at the core of the farmworker movement. Some merchants along the corridor have raised practical concerns about the cost of updating signage and business materials. City officials previously estimated replacing street signs and related markings would run about $107,000. Board President Mandelman waived the standard 30-day waiting period, meaning a vote could be scheduled as soon as November 4.

topStories.headline: After Six Years and $37 Million, the Mission Branch Library Is Ready to Come Home
topStories.dek: The landmark Carnegie building at 24th and Bartlett will reopen November 14 with a restored entrance, a new teen room, a courtyard, and solar panels — after a renovation that took three times longer than planned.
topStories.body:
The Mission Branch Library — the oldest branch in the San Francisco Public Library system, housed in a Carnegie-funded building that opened in 1915 — will reopen on Saturday, November 14, at 1 p.m. after more than six years of closure and a renovation that ultimately cost roughly $37 million.

The building at 300 Bartlett Street, on the corner of 24th Street, shut in March 2020. Actual construction did not begin until August 2023, and the project ran approximately a year past its most recent completion target. Delays stemmed from unforeseen field conditions, additional structural design work, neighbors' concerns about shoring and pinning of the structure, and a prolonged wait for PG&E to de-energize an electrical vault on the site.

The renovated library includes a new room dedicated to teens and young-adult books, a children's room, a community meeting room that seats 100, a new outdoor courtyard, and two additional bathrooms. The building received a full seismic retrofit and has been taken entirely off natural gas, with solar panels installed on the roof. A grand interior staircase on the 24th Street side — removed in a 1997 renovation — has been rebuilt, and the library's original 24th Street entrance has been restored after nearly three decades of disuse.

During construction, the branch has operated from a temporary space around the corner at 1234 Valencia Street. The San Francisco Public Library says a community celebration with Aztec dancers, a children's story hour, and live music will mark the reopening on November 14. The temporary Valencia Street location will close once the main building is back in service.

topStories.headline: A 45-Story Tower Is Proposed for the Mission's Last Car Wash
topStories.dek: Developer Manna Capital filed preliminary permits for a 479-foot, 528-unit rental skyscraper at 1601 Mission Street — a triangular lot that has seen ambitious proposals come and go for decades.
topStories.body:
Preliminary permits filed October 7 call for a 45-story residential skyscraper at 1601 Mission Street, where the Tower Car Wash occupies a triangular lot near South Van Ness Avenue. Chicago-based developer Manna Capital is the project sponsor. If built, the 479-foot structure would rank among the largest housing projects in San Francisco since the pandemic.

The building, designed by Solomon Cordwell Buenz, would contain 528 rental apartments across roughly 542,800 square feet of residential space. The unit mix ranges from 114 studios to 20 three-bedroom apartments. Amenities planned for the sixth floor, the 45th floor, and a rooftop deck include a spa, outdoor swimming pool, yoga studio, co-working lounge, and a golf simulator room. The ground floor would include 900 square feet of retail, and a podium garage would hold 190 cars.

Of the 528 units, 80 would be deed-restricted as affordable housing — 40 for very low-income households and 40 for moderate-income households — a requirement tied to the project's use of California's Assembly Bill 1287, Senate Bill 330, and the state density bonus program. Those tools allow the developer to more than double what was previously envisioned for the site: an 11-story, 220-unit condominium building first proposed in 2014.

The property sold in October 2024 for $12 million. Estimated construction costs are roughly $312 million. The project is in the earliest permitting stage and faces a lengthy planning and approval process before any ground could break.

events.title: Invisible Atlas — Ranko Ogura Dance at Dance Mission Theater
events.location: Dance Mission Theater, 3316 24th St., Mission District
events.description: Ranko Ogura Dance presents an immersive multimedia performance blending Butoh and contemporary dance with poetry, projected animation, and live shakuhachi and taiko drumming. Drawing on the nuclear legacies of Hiroshima, Nagasaki, and Fukushima, the work asks how invisible environmental damage echoes across generations. Tickets $20–$65.

events.title: Alemany Farm's 21st Annual Harvest Festival
events.location: Alemany Farm, 700 Alemany Blvd., Outer Mission
events.description: The Friends of Alemany Farm, the Bernal Heights Neighborhood Center, and partner organizations host this free, all-ages community celebration with garlic planting, guided farm tours, live music, face painting, and a community meal. Donations welcome; no on-site parking — street parking available on Alemany Blvd.

events.title: 18th Cine+Más SF Latino Film Festival
events.location: Roxie Theater, 3117 16th St., and Artists' Television Access, 992 Valencia St., Mission District, plus other SF venues
events.description: The 18th annual San Francisco Latino Film Festival presents roughly 50 features, documentaries, and shorts from across Latin America, Spain, and the United States, with a geo-fenced virtual program for Bay Area residents running October 26 through November 5. The festival opened October 22 at the Roxie with a documentary on Sesame Street actress Sonia Manzano.

events.title: Halloween & Día de los Muertos Market at Mission Community Market
events.location: Mission Community Market, 22nd Street at Bartlett St. and 84 Bartlett St., Mission District
events.description: The weekly Mission Community Market goes festive for Halloween and Día de los Muertos with fall produce, marigolds, papel picado, a community ofrenda honoring ancestors, live music, and family activities. Free to attend; costumes welcome for all ages.

events.title: Mission Branch Library Reopening Celebration
events.location: Mission Branch Library, 300 Bartlett St. at 24th Street, Mission District
events.description: The San Francisco Public Library marks the return of the renovated Mission Branch with a community celebration featuring Aztec dancers, a children's story hour, and live music. The historic Carnegie building has been closed since March 2020; the temporary branch at 1234 Valencia Street will close once the main building reopens.

moreNews.headline: City to Fast-Track $1.8 Million in Emergency Immigrant Legal Aid
moreNews.body:
District 9 Supervisor Jackie Fielder — whose district covers the Mission — announced at a City Hall rally on Tuesday, October 20, that San Francisco would commit $1.8 million in emergency supplemental funding for immigrant legal defense. The move came one day after surveillance video showed masked ICE agents conducting a forceful street arrest in SoMa. All 11 supervisors and Mayor Daniel Lurie expressed support for the measure, and Board President Rafael Mandelman waived the standard 30-day waiting period, making a vote possible as soon as November 4.

The money would fund immigration attorneys, accompaniment services for people attending ICE appointments, and the city's rapid-response hotline. Among the expected recipients is La Raza Centro Legal, headquartered in the Mission, and the Bay Area Habeas Network — a coalition of nine legal nonprofits and public defenders' offices that has filed emergency court petitions securing the release of more than 50 detained Bay Area residents since May.
